title: A water utility's revenue requirement, year by year

blocks.text: A small water utility (a fictional one) asks its commission for rates. Its pipe and plant additions are placed in service at the start of a year, and the commission in this exercise uses three conventions:

items: **Straight-line depreciation** over a book life of `life` years: an addition of cost $`C`$ is depreciated $`C / \text{life}`$ in its first year of service and in each following year until its life is over, and never after.

**End-of-year rate base**: in year $`y`$, each addition counts at its cost less all the depreciation charged on it up to and including year $`y`$, and never below zero. An addition not yet in service is not in the rate base.
**Operating expenses** (O&M) are recovered in the year they are spent, dollar for dollar.

blocks.text: Write `revenue_requirement(additions, life, rate, om, years)` in `rates.py`. `additions` maps the year an addition is placed in service to its cost ($k), `rate` is the allowed rate of return, `om` maps a year to that year's O&M ($k, a missing year is 0), and the result maps each year of `years` to its revenue requirement:

Before you code, work one case by hand: $1,000k placed in 2027, a 4-year life and a 10% return. What are 2027's depreciation, rate base and revenue requirement, and what is 2031's? Then decide how one addition's age in year $`y`$ tells you whether it depreciates, and how much of it is left in the rate base.

This exercise's rate base is the **end-of-year** one, not the lesson's. `revenue_requirement.py` takes the average of each year's opening and closing net plant, the convention the lesson's source calls usual; this commission uses the closing value alone, which is also a convention a commission may set, and which keeps each year's arithmetic to one subtraction. The two differ: for the $1,000k case above, 2027's rate base is $750k at year end and $875k on average, so the requirement is $325k here and would be $337.5k with the lesson's average. The tests use the end-of-year values.
The tests compare your numbers with values worked out by hand. About fifteen lines.

"""Run executes this file. Change the calls and see what prints. Submit grades."""
import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from rates import revenue_requirement

years = [2030, 2031, 2032, 2033, 2034]
one = revenue_requirement({2030: 1_200}, 3, 0.08, {}, years)
print("1200 placed 2030, life 3, rate 8%:", {y: round(v, 2) for y, v in one.items()})
two = revenue_requirement({2030: 1_200, 2031: 600}, 3, 0.08, {2031: 50}, years)
print("plus 600 in 2031 and O&M 50 in 2031:", {y: round(v, 2) for y, v in two.items()})

cases.says: one addition's depreciation and end-of-year return in its first years
additions placed in different years each add their own depreciation and return
an addition past its book life adds no depreciation and no return
an addition adds nothing to the years before it is placed in service
operating expenses are recovered once, with no return on them

origin.section: A Rate Case Turns Capital Into Rates Through the Rate Base

concepts: capital spend is recovered over an asset's life with a return, while operating spend is recovered in its year
the revenue requirement is the rate base times the rate of return plus operating expenses, with the rate base net of depreciation
